items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: When you calculate 17.3/6.89 you actually obtain 2.51. When doing these calculations it is fine to round 2.51 to 2.5 or 1.01 to 1 but what you must not do is round 2.51 to 3!

items.label: text
items.text: If you got a ratio of C:H of 1:1.33 you would not round this down to 1:1 but rather multiply by 3 to obtain C3H.

items.label: text
items.text: The percentage figures apply to any amount of substance you choose, so let's choose 100 g. In this case the percentages convert simply into masses: 82.7% of 100 g is 82.7g (Table 5.1).

items.label: text
items.text: Table 5.1 Finding the ratio from percentage by mass

items.label: text
items.text: From this we can see that there are 2.5 mol of H atoms for every mole of C atoms. The empirical formula, however, is the whole number ratio of the elements present in a compound. To obtain a whole number here we multiply both numbers by 2 to get C2H₅, which is the empirical formula.

items.label: section_header
items.text: CONVERTING EMPIRICAL FORMULAE INTO MOLECULAR FORMULAE

items.label: text
items.text: When you have learned a bit more organic chemistry in Unit 4 you will realise that, in the example we have just looked at, C2H5 can't possibly be the real formula of the compound. The molecular formula (the actual number of each atom present in a molecule) has to be a multiple of C2H5, like C4H10.

items.label: text
items.text: We can find the molecular formula if we know the relative formula mass of the compound (or the mass of 1 mole, which is just the M, in grams).

items.label: text
items.text: In the previous example, suppose you were told that the relative formula mass of the compound was58.

items.label: text
items.text: C2H5 has a relative formula mass of 29 (A, of H = 1, A, of C = 12).

items.label: text
items.text: All you need to find out is how many times 29 goes into 58.

items.label: text
items.text: So you need 2 lots of C2H5, in other words, C4H10-

items.label: text
items.text: The molecular formula is C4H10-

items.label: section_header
items.text: EXAMPLE 6

items.label: text
items.text: A compound has the empirical formula CH2. If the relative formula mass is 56, work out the molecular formula.

items.label: text
items.text: The relative formula mass of CH2 is 12 + (2 × 1) = 14.

items.label: text
items.text: Therefore there must be 4 lots of CH2 in the actual molecule and the molecular formula is CH8.

items.label: text
items.text: Remember, the ratio of elements in the molecular formula must be the same as in the empirical formula: C4H8 cancels down to CH2.
